sign and Analysis of Algorithms
Purpose and Expected Standard

This handbook provides fifty substantial projects that translate the complete Design and Analysis of Algorithms syllabus into industry-oriented C or C++ products. Every project is designed for an eight-week development period and requires students to move beyond a single algorithm: they must model a real problem, implement alternative strategies, prove or justify correctness, measure time and space behaviour, and explain which approach is practical under different operating conditions.
The title, ten-point explanation, and expected product for every project are self-contained. The Common Syllabus Implementation Standard below is mandatory for every
student
and forms part of every project
briefly
, even when a domain naturally emphasizes only some algorithms.
Common Syllabus Implementation Standard for Every Project
Syllabus area
Mandatory evidence in the submission
Algorithm foundations and analysis

Define inputs, outputs, constraints, invariants and edge cases; document algorithm characteristics; collect operation counts, execution time and memory use; express best, average and worst cases with O, Ω and Θ notation.
Recurrence relations
Formulate and solve recurrences for selected recursive modules using iteration, substitution, recursion trees and the Master Theorem, stating when the theorem is not applicable.
Divide and conquer

Implement and benchmark iterative and recursive binary search, merge sort, quick sort, a maximum-subarray analysis, fast exponentiation, celebrity identification, and classical versus Strassen matrix multiplication using project data or a mapped analytical subproblem.
Greedy methods

Use activity selection or interval partitioning for scheduling, fractional-knapsack reasoning for prioritized allocation, Huffman coding for compression, Dijkstra for non-negative shortest paths, and Prim and Kruskal for minimum spanning infrastructure.
Dynamic programming

Implement 0/1 knapsack, matrix-chain multiplication, longest common subsequence, optimal binary search tree, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall and a small-instance travelling salesperson solver; compare dynamic programming with divide-and-conquer and greedy choices.
Backtracking and branch and bound

Implement N-Queens as a constraint-solving validation exercise, sum of subsets, 0/1 knapsack by backtracking, and FIFO, LIFO and least-cost branch-and-bound variants for knapsack or travelling salesperson decisions.
Flow and matching
Model a capacity network and implement Ford-Fulkerson; derive a maximum bipartite matching module for assignment between two entity groups.
Number and polynomial representation
Implement a Chinese Remainder Theorem utility and demonstrate at least one project-relevant use such as
distributed counters, modular verification, hashing experiments or reconstruction of partitioned results.
String matching
Implement and compare naive matching, Rabin-Karp, finite-automaton matching and Knuth-Morris-Pratt on domain text, identifiers, event streams or encoded sequences.
Complexity classes and reducibility
Classify major decision versions as P, NP, NP-complete or NP-hard where defensible; provide one clear polynomial-time reduction argument or mapping for the project’s difficult optimization component.
Required Engineering Practices
Use C17 or C++17 or later, modular source files, clear interfaces, defensive input validation and deterministic builds with Make or CMake.
Do not use library calls as replacements for the required core algorithms; standard containers may be used, but the assessed algorithms must be implemented and tested by the
student
Provide automated unit tests, integration tests, adversarial cases and reproducible benchmark datasets of increasing size.
Separate the domain model, algorithm implementations, experiment runner, persistence layer and user interface so that algorithms can be swapped fairly.
Record correctness evidence, empirical complexity graphs or tables, limitations, ethical or safety concerns, and a reasoned algorithm-selection guide.
Maintain a Git repository with issues, branches, meaningful commits, code review evidence, release tags and a concise installation guide.
Suggested
Eight-Week
Execution Plan
Period
Milestone
Week 1
Requirements, datasets, constraints, use cases, architecture and baseline tests.
Week 2
Analysis framework, sorting, searching, recurrences and divide-and-conquer modules.
Week 3
Greedy scheduling, compression, shortest path and spanning-tree modules.
Week 4
Dynamic programming modules and first cross-paradigm comparison.
Week 5
Backtracking, branch-and-bound, pruning and exact small-instance solvers.
Week 6
Maximum flow, bipartite matching, CRT and string-matching modules.
Week 7
Integration, complexity classification, reduction argument, stress tests and optimization.
Week 8
Final validation, documentation, demonstration, viva preparation and release packaging.
